bib.title: Model measurement and why it's so important (Chapter 11, Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: How should an ML team measure and report a deployed model's impact in business metrics, and which statistical tests fit an A/B attribution analysis?

limits: Book chapter: all data are simulated for illustration; no empirical results from a real deployment.
The chapter's sample-size and test code assumes normality and balanced groups for the power calculation; nonparametric power is not covered.
Bias measurement is mentioned as required for customer-facing models but not covered.
Drift detection is deferred to the next chapter.
Listings use deprecated or fragile calls (matplotlib 'seaborn' style, wilcoxon on unpaired samples).
practices: Report model impact in the business's own metrics (revenue, coupon usage), not ML loss metrics; keep both for the project's lifetime (p.310-311).
Agree the business metric definitions with the team that already computes them (finance, operations, QA) (p.331-332).
Talk to SMEs before release and ask what OKRs and queries they use to judge success (p.332).
Use random sampling within strata (RFM meta-groups) to balance control and test and cut within-group variance (p.305-308).
Do not let one group be badly unbalanced between control and test, e.g. 90% of top-RFM customers in control (thought exercise, p.308).
Compute required sample size and time to a conclusive result before release and tell the business (p.317-319).
Fix the evaluation rules and a monitoring job for significance tests in advance; do not read early daily deltas (Fig 11.11, p.320).
Check normality (plot a density) before choosing between parametric and nonparametric tests; revenue is often heavy-tailed (Fig 11.12, p.321).
Use Mann-Whitney U for non-stationary or non-normal series; ANOVA/t-test only for stationary normal data (p.323-324).
Use Tukey HSD for pairwise comparisons among many groups (p.327).
Use Fisher's exact or chi-square for happen/not-happen metrics (p.329).
Never claim causation from model correlations or from a significant A/B result alone; an A/B test only rejects equivalence and shows the predictions are useful (p.310, 316).

Scale monitoring to criticality: standard ML metrics for internal tooling; drift detection for decision-critical internal models; attribution, drift and bias detection for customer-facing models (p.323).
When several changes ship together, accept the confounding, release the best solution first and run variation tests later (p.317).
